title: The metric is an unweighted mean, so our two worst labels are worth +0.0173 - above the bar
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-11 from the whole-stack fold-0 member (mean 0.8457), using the per-label table RunMetrics now records every epoch.

THE ARITHMETIC THAT MAKES THIS THE BIGGEST LEVER ON THE BOARD: the competition metric is the UNWEIGHTED mean of twelve per-label ROC AUCs. A point of AUC on MCL is worth exactly as much as a point on Effusion. Our labels are not close to level:

  MCL              0.755   <- worst
  Fracture         0.784
  Lateral OA       0.822
  PF OA            0.824
  ...
  Medial Meniscus  0.893
  Baker's          0.896   <- best

Lifting a label to 0.873 - a level we demonstrably reach on five others - is worth (0.873 - x)/12 on the mean:
  MCL      +0.0098
  Fracture +0.0074
  bottom two together  +0.0173, which is ABOVE the 1.5% bar and larger than whole-stack (+0.0147).

TWO EXPLANATIONS TESTED AND BOTH REFUTED, which is what makes this actionable rather than a shrug:
  - NOT RARITY. Synovitis has 580 positives (13.2%), FEWER than MCL's 767 (17.4%), and scores 0.873 against MCL's 0.755.
  - NOT LABEL NOISE. Synovitis has the LOWEST mean reader confidence in the corpus (0.189) and still scores 0.873; MCL has high confidence (0.789) and scores worst. Baker's at confidence 0.508 is our BEST label at 0.896.
So neither how often a finding occurs nor how sure the report reader was predicts how well we do. MCL is HARD TO SEE. That is an imaging problem, and it contradicts this project's standing 'supervision-limited' thesis for at least this label.

WHERE THAT POINTS: the MCL is a thin structure at the MEDIAL MARGIN of the field, read coronally. A 130 mm crop at 336 px is 0.39 mm per pixel, and the occlusion test already showed centre-only and border-only scoring the same, i.e. no privileged reading of the joint centre. knee-dft (336 -> 448) carries a pre-registered prediction that any gain must CONCENTRATE in ACL/MCL/meniscus - it now has a named target with measured headroom, which makes it a sharper experiment than when it was filed.

FRACTURE IS PROBABLY A DIFFERENT PROBLEM: 7.1% prevalence and confidence 0.406 - both low. Marrow oedema needs fluid-sensitive fat-suppressed sequences, which we do route. Worth separating from MCL rather than treating 'the two worst labels' as one thing.

WHAT NOT TO DO, per the house rule: do not reweight the loss toward the weak labels. 'Keep the objective general - never fit it to a specific weakness; fix needs with balanced data, not loss-engineering.' If a balance fix is warranted it belongs in SAMPLING - oversampling studies carrying rare positives - not in per-label loss weights, and it should be justified by prevalence, which the numbers above say is NOT the problem here anyway.

title: Attend across slices instead of maxing them: the published successor to what just worked
description:
PRIOR ART, found 2026-08-11 after whole-stack paid off. Medical Slice Transformer (Nature Scientific Reports 2025) encodes each slice with a 2D encoder - DINOv2, the same backbone we use - and then runs a SLICE TRANSFORMER with attention across slices, plus within-slice patch attention. A two-stage transformer with a [CLS] token over the slice sequence appears in the same literature, and Memory-Guided Transformer (Pattern Recognition 2025) adds group attention across anatomical planes, reporting best-in-class on MRNet.

WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT NEXT ARM RATHER THAN A NEW IDEA: we have just measured that seeing every slice per step is worth +0.0147, our largest change, using the crudest possible aggregation - an elementwise maximum. Max keeps, per feature dimension, whichever slice shouted loudest and discards which slice it was and everything the others said. Attention over the same axis keeps the axis.

THE CHANGE IS SMALL AND LOCAL. model.py slot_features already encodes each slice separately under slice_pooling='max' and ends with:
    pooled.reshape(batch, slots, group, -1).amax(dim=2)
The slice axis is right there. Replacing amax with a learned attention over dim=2 - a query per diagnosis, or a single shared query to start - is a contained edit behind a new slice_pooling value, so every existing member keeps loading.

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE FROM OUR OWN MEASUREMENTS:
  - the occlusion depth profile spans 0.7976..0.8332 across windows, so WHICH slice matters, and max deliberately throws that away.
  - SlotHead already does exactly this trick one level up (per-diagnosis query attention over slots, masked) and it works. This is the same mechanism applied to the axis below it.
  - the depth-by-label diagnostic exists to say whether labels want different depths; if they do, a per-diagnosis slice query is the correct shape rather than a shared one.

RISK, stated up front: it adds parameters to a model this project has repeatedly called supervision-limited, and 58 image-read labels is not much to fit an attention with. The anatomical prior - forcing correct slot attention - measured neutral, which is evidence that MORE attention machinery is not automatically better here. Start with a single shared query, not per-diagnosis.

RUN ORDER: after tonight's folds, and after knee-gtw (20 slices under whole-stack), which is cheaper and tests the same axis by adding evidence rather than parameters.

title: Slice count is UNREFUTED under whole-stack: the old test only ruled it out for windowed reading
description:
THE REFUTATION WE HAVE DOES NOT COVER THIS CASE, and the distinction is mechanical.

WHAT WAS REFUTED (knee-ezz, closed): 20 cached slices against 12, both read as ONE RANDOM 3-SLICE WINDOW per step. 0.8309 vs 0.8310 - nothing. It could not have worked: at a fixed group of 3 the window covers 3 slices however many are cached, so more slices only changes which window can be drawn, not what a step sees.

WHY WHOLE-STACK CHANGES THE QUESTION: whole-stack reads EVERY cached slice per slot per step, so the cached slice count IS the anatomy a step sees - 12 slices is 72 images per study, 20 is 120. No window, no group to thin. The mechanism that made the old arm null is absent.

SUPPORT: whole-stack itself is +0.0147 and its mechanism is exactly 'see more of the stack'; the occlusion depth profile spans 0.7976..0.8332; the 0.20-0.80 band holds ~18 slices on the median study and we keep 12; MRNet maxes over ALL slices, not a fixed 12. The 20-slice cache is already built (59.7 GB), so this costs no decode.

THE BLOCKER, measured rather than assumed: whole-stack at batch 12 with 12 slices puts 864 images through the encoder and holds 19.2 GB with gradient checkpointing on. Twenty slices is 1440 images, about 1.7x, so roughly 33 GB - MORE THAN THE 32 GB CARD. This arm cannot run as a drop-in.

THE THREE WAYS OUT, and none is free:
  1. Batch 8 instead of 12: ~960 images, fits in ~22 GB. But the ranking term scores pairs WITHIN a batch - 66 pairs at 12, 28 at 8 - so it changes the objective, and the arm would no longer be single-variable against tonight's folds.
  2. Cache 16 slices rather than 20: ~1150 images, ~26 GB. Fits, keeps the batch, and still recovers most of the band's median 18 slices. Costs one decode pass (~40 min, CPU).
  3. Accept the whole card and drop coexistence with the other project for the duration.

RECOMMENDED: (2). It keeps the batch and therefore the objective, it tests the same mechanism, and the decode is CPU work that can run while the GPU does something else. Sixteen is also closer to what the band actually holds than twenty.

RUN AFTER tonight's folds.

title: Whole-stack peaks at epoch 9 of 24, so its epoch budget is wrong
description:
CONFIRMED 2026-08-11, and the shorter budget scored HIGHER rather than merely cheaper.

  whole-stack, 24 epochs: best 0.8413, peak at epoch 6
  whole-stack, 12 epochs: best 0.8457, peak at epoch 6

Same peak LOCATION, better peak VALUE, half the wall-clock. The peak epoch is a property of how much the model sees per step, not of the schedule length - 4x the imaging per step means convergence around epoch 6 either way.

WHY THE SHORTER RUN SCORES BETTER, which is the part that is not obvious: one-cycle is defined over total_steps. A 24-epoch budget stretches warmup and decay across epochs the model does not need, so at the epoch where it actually converges the learning rate is still far from annealed. Matching the budget to the convergence point makes the anneal land where the model is.

So an inflated epoch budget is not a harmless waste of GPU - it detunes the schedule. That reframes the 8 -> 24 epoch result from earlier today: that gain was measured on the WINDOWED recipe, which needs the longer budget because it sees a quarter as much per step. The budget belongs to the recipe, not to the project.

APPLIED: experiments/arms/whole_stack.sh and wholestack_folds.sh both run 12 epochs.
NOT YET TESTED: 8 epochs, which the peak-at-6 suggests might do as well again. Left alone tonight because folds 1-3 must stay matched to fold 0 for the ensemble to mean anything.

title: Give VRAM back to the other project: find the smallest batch that still saturates compute
description:
OWNER'S FRAMING, 2026-08-11, and it is the right one: VRAM is a HARD partition (oversubscribe it and Windows pages over PCIe, which is how a 32 GB run ended up at 145 W of 575 doing nothing), while compute is time-sliced. So the objective is the SMALLEST memory footprint that still saturates the SMs - the free space is worth real money to the other project on this card, and the utilisation is shared anyway.

WHERE WE ARE, measured under whole-stack at batch 12 with checkpointing and an 18 GB cap:
  VRAM 19.2 GB | utilisation 95-100% | power 540-556 W of 575 (96%) | CPU 12%
That is COMPUTE-limited, unambiguously. A memory-limited run looks like the uncapped version of the same arm: 100% 'utilisation' at 145 W with 1% memory-controller traffic.

THE SWEEP, to run when the GPU is free: batch 12 / 8 / 6 / 4 at fixed everything else, recording peak VRAM, power, utilisation and seconds per epoch. Expected shape - VRAM falls sublinearly because weights, optimiser states, CUDA context and the checkpoint boundaries are fixed costs, so batch 6 lands near 12-13 GB rather than 9.6; power and utilisation hold until the batch gets small enough to go launch-bound.

MUST BE MEASURED ALONE. A second process on the card time-shares the SMs, so both would report ~100% utilisation and the reading would say nothing about either.

THE CAVEAT THAT STOPS THIS BEING A FREE KNOB: batch size is not neutral to the OBJECTIVE. The ranking term scores pairs WITHIN a batch - 66 pairs at batch 12, 15 at batch 6 - so shrinking the batch weakens the exact term we added deliberately. Any batch chosen for memory reasons has to be re-measured on score, not assumed equivalent. The lever that IS free is gradient checkpointing, already applied: 32 GB -> 19 GB with the loss untouched.

OUTPUT: a recommended (batch, vram-gb) pair per arm shape, recorded in experiments/README.md so arms declare a budget rather than taking what they find.

title: Resolution: 336 px for findings a few voxels wide, with a per-label prediction that makes it falsifiable
description:
MECHANISM THAT COULD PLAUSIBLY CLEAR 1.5%, now with PUBLISHED COUNTER-EVIDENCE recorded before the run.

THE ARM: 336 -> 448 px, everything else held. Cost is quadratic in bytes and step time; the cache is keyed by resolution so 336 px members stay reproducible. Needs --recompute-activations (gradient checkpointing) or it overflows 32 GB and thrashes.

THE ORIGINAL ARGUMENT: we read a 130 mm crop at 336 px, so a pixel is ~0.39 mm, while a meniscal tear or cruciate fibre discontinuity is millimetre-scale. Five of twelve targets are meniscus or ligament. Occlusion (knee-am4) shows centre-only 0.8021 against border-only 0.8006 and whole 0.8448, which is what a model leaning on coarse global context looks like.

COUNTER-EVIDENCE, found 2026-08-11 while reading prior art rather than after the result: MRNet (Stanford, PLOS Medicine 2018) detects ACL tears at AUC ~0.97 using AlexNet at 256 px - LOWER resolution than ours. If millimetre findings were unresolvable at 0.39 mm/pixel, that result should not exist. My 'we cannot resolve fine anatomy' argument is therefore weaker than I stated it.

WHAT SURVIVES THE COUNTER-EVIDENCE: MRNet's task is three coarse labels on one institution's curated dataset with radiologist labels. Ours is twelve labels across 16 sites and 12 languages with 98.7% LLM-derived labels. Harder supervision and more heterogeneity could plausibly raise the resolution requirement. But that is a story, and the counter-example is a measurement.

THE PREDICTION STANDS AND IS NOW SHARPER: the gain must CONCENTRATE in ACL, MCL, Medial and Lateral Meniscus and be near zero for Effusion and Baker's. Given MRNet, the most likely outcome is now NO concentrated gain - and that would be a clean refutation rather than a disappointment, because it redirects to what MRNet says actually carries the signal (see knee-jk3 and the whole-stack arm).

PRIORITY UNCHANGED at P0 but ORDER CHANGED: run whole-stack FIRST. It has published support and this arm now has published doubt.
notes: 2026-08-11 20:34Z: arm re-pointed at whole-stack (12 epochs, control wsfold0_e6=0.8457, batch held at 12 so the ranking term's within-batch pair count does not move). 448px/12sl cache exists (63.7 GB) so the arm is unblocked. Queued behind fold 3 via experiments/after.sh; a stray /tmp/after_folds.sh gated on fold 2 was killed - it would have run resolution INTO fold 3, 21.6 GB each on a 32 GB card.

title: We are 0.054 off the frontier because we replicated a design that discards ~90% of the data
description:
DIAGNOSIS 2026-08-11, after the owner asked why two days of work moved the public score so little.

WHERE WE ARE: LB 0.888, rank 367 of 1077. Public median 0.819, leader 0.942. We clear the median and sit around the 34th percentile. The gap to the frontier is 0.054 - THIRTY TIMES the size of every lever measured on 2026-08-11 (rate +0.0051, pooling +0.0038, ranking +0.005).

IT IS NOT A BUG. The one real bug - augmentation silently disabled - was found and fixed and was worth +0.020, more than every method change since combined. No second defect of that size is visible.

IT IS NOT MAINLY THE REGIMEN, though ours is thin: pilkwang trains 60 epochs x 20 members, we train 24 x 5. Worth something; not worth 0.054. Per MEMBER we are competitive - five of ours equal twenty of theirs on the leaderboard.

THE ACTUAL CAUSE: we replicated pilkwang's design and then optimised inside it. That design discards most of the available data, and our own beads hold every number:
  - a training step sees 18 of ~180 acquired slices (6 slots x 3 consecutive) [knee-hek]
  - we cache 12 slices per series out of a median 30 [knee-ezz]
  - 4,241 series - 17.4% - never reach a slot at all, because there are six fixed slots [knee-t92]
  - 336 px, for findings like meniscal tears that are a few voxels across

Every arm run on 2026-08-11 was a knob INSIDE that family. A knob inside a family returns ~0.005 by construction. That is not bad luck, and it should have been said before running them rather than after.

THE TARGETING ERROR THAT LET IT HAPPEN, already recorded in comp/SUBMISSIONS.md:54 - '0.899 was taken from a public notebook's title and called the plateau; on the actual leaderboard 0.899 is about 100th place and the frontier is 0.942'. We anchored on the best PUBLISHED artefact and treated it as SOTA.

WHY THERE WAS NOTHING BETTER TO ANCHOR ON: the competition is LIVE - it runs to 2026-10-22 with winners in November - so no top-solution write-ups exist. 'Gather SOTA then replicate' has no SOTA to gather here. That is a real constraint, and it means the frontier has to be reached by reasoning about the data rather than by copying.

IT ALSO EXPLAINS THE BORDER RESULT (knee-am4). A model scoring 0.8006 from the periphery alone, with the centre adding nothing, behaves like a model that CANNOT RESOLVE fine anatomy and is leaning on coarse global context. That is the signature of the data starvation above, not a separate pathology. The two findings are one finding.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PLAN: stop running knob arms. Only run arms whose mechanism could plausibly deliver 1.5% - all of them are about showing the model more of what it was given.

title: Depth spread across windows is 0.036 - larger than every method change combined, and we sample uniformly
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-11 by occlusion on base+ranking (experiments/arms/attribution.sh), each 3-slice window scored ALONE over 400 holdout studies:
  best single window starts at slice 7 = 0.8332
  range 0.7976 .. 0.8332 across the ten windows, SPREAD 0.0356

For scale: the whole model with all ten windows averaged scores 0.8448, and the best SINGLE window gets to 0.8332 on its own. The spread across depth is larger than every method change this project has ever measured put together (rate +0.0051, pooling +0.0038, ranking +0.005, base encoder +0.0085).

WHAT WE DO WITH THAT TODAY: nothing. trainer.py draws ONE uniform random window start per batch, so steps are spent evenly across depths - including the ones worth 0.798. And Trainer.predict scores epochs on the MIDDLE window, which is not the best window (slice 7 of a 0..9 start range is off-centre).

THREE CANDIDATE MOVES, in increasing cost and increasing risk of fooling ourselves:
  1. INFERENCE, free: weight the ten TTA windows by their measured value instead of averaging uniformly. Risk: the weights are fitted on the holdout, so they must be cross-validated per fold or they are just holdout overfitting. Do NOT ship a weighting fitted on the same fold it is scored on.
  2. TRAINING, cheap: sample window starts non-uniformly toward the informative band. This is a curriculum, not a leak - the model still sees every depth, just not equally.
  3. UNDERSTAND IT FIRST. Is slice 7 special because of anatomy (the intercondylar notch, the cruciates) or because of the 0.20-0.80 band's geometry? The profile should be re-measured per LABEL - a meniscus finding and an effusion have no reason to share a best depth, and a per-label profile would say whether one window can serve all twelve.

(3) gates the others: a single global best-window is only worth acting on if the labels agree, and per-label profiles cost one more occlusion pass with no training.

RELATED: this is the same evidence that motivates whole-stack reading (knee-hek), from the opposite direction - that arm removes the window choice entirely rather than optimising it.

title: Border-only scores 0.8006 of a 0.8448 model - the centre of the joint carries nothing privileged
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-11 by occlusion on base+ranking, 400 holdout studies (experiments/arms/attribution.sh):
  whole 0.8448 | centre-only 0.8021 | border-only 0.8006

The diagnostic's own docstring says border-only should be near chance. It is not. Keeping ONLY the outer region recovers 95% of the full score, and centre-only beats it by 0.0015 - inside noise. The centre of the joint carries nothing the periphery does not.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT YET PROVE. 'Border' here is the image minus the central 50%x50% square, which is 75% of the AREA and still contains a great deal of joint anatomy - the crop is 130 mm around the joint, so the central quarter-area is only the very middle. So the result is consistent with two very different worlds:
  (a) the signal is diffuse and redundant across the field - benign, and would predict that a model reading any large fraction of the knee does well;
  (b) the model is reading the periphery - coil, soft tissue, burned-in laterality marker or vendor text - which is a shortcut that would not survive a different scanner population.
The test as designed cannot separate them, and that is the defect worth fixing first.

WHY IT IS A P0 DESPITE BEING AMBIGUOUS: if (b) holds even partly, it caps generalisation to the hidden test set in a way no amount of encoder tuning addresses, and every gain measured this session was measured on a ruler that shares the artefact. It is also the only hypothesis on the board whose mechanism could plausibly be worth more than 1.5%.

THE SHARPER TESTS, cheapest first:
  1. A NARROW RING. Keep only the outer 10-15% of the field, which on a 130 mm crop is almost entirely outside the joint. If that alone still scores well above chance the answer is (b).
  2. LOOK AT THE PIXELS. Dump the border ring for a handful of studies and check for burned-in text or laterality markers - the DICOM tags will also say (BurnedInAnnotation, ImageComments).
  3. If (b): train with the ring blanked and see what the holdout does. A model that loses little is reading anatomy after all.

Cheap: no training, one occlusion pass each.

title: Gate the reader work: what is the existing severity gradation actually worth?
description:
BEFORE investing in a better report reader that emits true ordinal severity, measure what the gradation we ALREADY have is worth. Cost-tiered: a cheap proxy gates the expensive commit.

THE ABLATION: report_labels_v2 carries three YES levels (0.68 / 0.82 / 0.94, 9,702 pairs). flatyes_v2.csv collapses all three to 0.82 - the middle level, so the average pull on a YES pair is unchanged - and changes NOTHING else. NO stays 0.08, UNK stays 0.28. The eval table is held fixed at the graded original so the ruler cannot move.

WHY THE RANKING TERM IS ON FOR THIS ARM: it is the only component that consumes the gradation (pair weight relu(s_i - s_j)); BCE mostly pulls both toward present and our local evaluation binarises at 0.5, collapsing the levels anyway. Running the ablation without ranking would test a channel nothing reads.

WHAT THE ANSWER BUYS:
  - If flattening COSTS materially: gradation is live signal, and a reader emitting true severity (grade 1/2/3, mild/moderate/severe) is worth building - the levels we have are a crude version of something that pays.
  - If flattening costs ~nothing: the three levels are assertion-strength the model cannot use, and a reader upgrade must supply genuinely NEW information (findings we do not extract at all) rather than finer grades. That would redirect the effort rather than cancel it.

EVIDENCE THAT MOTIVATED IT: a linear probe on the report embedding separates 0.94 from 0.68 at mean AUC 0.730 over 9,702 pairs (Effusion 0.845, ACL 0.813, Synovitis 0.576). So the levels are driven by report CONTENT, not by sampling noise. That says they are real; it does not say the IMAGE can see them, which is what this arm tests.
close_reason: GATE PASSED. Collapsing the three YES levels to one costs -0.0044 (0.8228 vs 0.8272) with ranking on and the eval table held graded. So the gradation we already have is signal the model can USE, not assertion-strength it ignores - which is the condition this issue set for investing in a reader that emits true ordinal severity. That work is knee-mxj, now unblocked by evidence rather than by assumption. Committed as experiments/arms/severity_flat.sh. Caveat kept: -0.0044 is under the 1.5% bar, so this licenses the effort, it does not promise the payoff.

title: Ordinal severity is the supervision that compounds with the ranking term
description:
OBSERVED in report_labels_v2: the labels are NOT binary. Verdict -> value: NO 0.08 (22,298 pairs), UNK 0.28 (14,445), YES 0.68 (6,461) / 0.82 (6,427) / 0.94 (3,241). Three graded levels already exist inside YES.

THE CONNECTION THAT MAKES THIS WORTH DOING: the pairwise ranking term is the ONLY component that consumes that gradation - its pair weight is relu(s_i - s_j), so a 0.94-vs-0.68 pair carries real signal. BCE mostly pulls both toward 'present', and our local evaluation binarises at MIDPOINT=0.5 and collapses the three levels entirely. Ranking is also the loss change that measured positive in 3/3 matched arms.

So finer severity is not just 'more supervision' - it compounds specifically with the mechanism that works, because the competition metric is a RANKING metric and severity is exactly a ranking signal. A model that knows a severe tear outranks a subtle one is being trained on the quantity being scored.

TWO SEPARATE UPGRADES, often conflated:
  (a) BETTER TEXT ENCODER for the auxiliary embedding target (knee-*, report supervision). Ours is sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 - a general paraphrase model, not medical. multilingual-e5-large or BGE-M3 are stronger multilingually; medical AND multilingual is rare, which matters across twelve languages.
  (b) BETTER READER producing ORDINAL targets - meniscal grade 1/2/3, mild/moderate/severe OA, partial vs full-thickness tear - rather than three certainty levels. This is the branch the label-FILTERING refutation explicitly did not kill: resolving a row is the opposite operation to striking it.

CHEAP FIRST TEST for (b) before any reader work: check whether the existing three YES levels carry ORDINAL information at all, by measuring whether studies labelled 0.94 are ranked above 0.68 studies by a trained model more often than chance. If the current levels are pure LLM certainty rather than severity, a reader upgrade has to supply real severity; if they already track severity, the gradation is a live signal we are only half-using.

NOTE the evaluation limit: our local ruler binarises at 0.5, so a finer target cannot be scored locally as ordinal - it can only be scored by whether it improves the binary AUC. That is the right test anyway, since the competition scores binary annotations.

title: Report-embedding supervision: we use 12 numbers where the report has hundreds of tokens
description:
THE BOTTLENECK, established today: the model is supervision-limited, not capacity-limited (large is +0.0021 over base and overfits by epoch 10). So the lever is more signal per study, and we are discarding most of what we have.

WHAT WE THROW AWAY: every study carries a full radiology report. We compress it to 12 graded numbers via an LLM label table and discard the rest - the anatomy named, the severity wording, the incidental findings, the negations, everything the twelve columns do not have a slot for. That is hundreds of tokens reduced to twelve.

THE METHOD (ConVIRT / GLoRIA / BioViL family, standard in medical imaging): embed each report with a multilingual text encoder ONCE, offline. Add an auxiliary head that predicts that embedding from the study representation, and train it jointly with the twelve-label loss. The image model is then supervised by the report's full content rather than by twelve extractions of it.

WHY IT IS LEGAL AND WHY IT FITS: test.csv has NO Report column, and this is exactly the setting the method assumes - text supervises at training time, inference is image-only. No external data, no licence question (knee-0s6 untouched).

WHY IT COULD BE WORTH PERCENT rather than a knob: it changes the AMOUNT of supervision, which is the constraint we just measured, rather than the capacity to absorb it, which we just measured as spent. It is also the one axis where our multilingual corpus is an ASSET instead of a liability - a multilingual encoder maps 'menisco medial roto' and 'medial meniscal tear' to nearby vectors, where our label reader has to parse both.

CHEAP FIRST TEST: multilingual sentence encoder -> per-report vector -> reduce to ~64 dims -> auxiliary cosine/MSE head at modest weight -> one small@24 arm against the 0.8272 ranking control. If the auxiliary loss trains at all and the number does not move, the idea is cheap to kill; if it moves, it scales to base and to the full-data fit.

RISK, stated: a multilingual encoder trained on general web text may embed radiology reports poorly, and 4,407 reports is a small target space. The failure mode is a useless auxiliary target that costs capacity - which is checkable by watching whether the auxiliary loss falls at all.
close_reason: REFUTED, and monotonically - which is what makes it a kill rather than a tuning miss. Report term at 0.3 = 0.8219, at 1.0 = 0.8209, control 0.8272. Both negative and MORE weight is MORE negative, so the weight is not the problem: forcing the slot embedding to predict a sentence-transformer embedding of the report actively costs the classifier. Mechanism: the report describes the whole study including everything the twelve labels already capture PLUS technique, history and incidental findings, so the auxiliary target pulls representation capacity toward text the metric never scores. The 12 numbers being fewer than the report's tokens was true and irrelevant. Encoder + report_embeddings.py + report_supervision.py stay in the tree, opt-in and default off.

title: Encoder learning rate: the axis the depth bracket could not see
description:
BACKBONE_LR = 8e-6 was a module constant with no CLI flag, so no run has ever varied it. The head:encoder ratio is 125:1.

WHY THIS INVALIDATES A RESULT I ALREADY REPORTED: the depth bracket (unfreeze 3 / 6 / 12) came out 0.8143 / 0.8205 / 0.8213. I read the 12-block arm as 'depth is a ceiling at 6'. But at 8e-6 the extra blocks barely move, so a null result cannot distinguish 'more trainable blocks do not help' from 'no block was going to move anyway'. The bracket measured adaptation capacity at a rate where adaptation does not happen.

Note the shallow arm still fell -0.0062, which says the rate is not so low that depth is irrelevant - only that the UPPER half of the bracket is uninformative.

MECHANISM FOR WHY THIS COULD BE WORTH PERCENT rather than a knob: DINOv2's features are natural-image features, and kneemri/trainer.py's own docstring says a frozen SSL encoder caps every downstream axis at once because nothing in natural images resembles a torn meniscus on a PD sequence. How far the encoder is allowed to move off those features is therefore the representation-capacity axis - and capacity is the only axis that has ever paid here.

ARMS (/tmp/chain15.sh), small + ranking @24, unfreeze 12, control rank24_s2026 = 0.8272:
  L: backbone 4e-5 (5x)
  M: backbone 1.6e-4 (20x)
Bracketed wide because the scale is unknown. Small rather than base because this is a signal test.

IF IT MOVES: re-run the depth bracket at the winning rate, since that result is currently uninterpretable, then take it to base. IF IT DOES NOT: the encoder is genuinely near its useful optimum under this supervision, and the next step up is domain-adaptive PRETRAINING on our own 24,371 series rather than a bigger fine-tuning rate.
close_reason: DUPLICATE, merged into knee-3om which holds the measurement: 8e-6 -> 0.8272, 4e-5 -> 0.8316 (+0.0044), 1.6e-4 -> ~0.739 collapsing. The 'IF IT MOVES' clause fired, and the re-run of the depth bracket at the winning rate is arm S/T, tracked in knee-3om. Nothing distinct left here.

title: Our ruler is a proxy: 58 annotated studies, so only the LB can arbitrate
description:
MEASURED: train.csv carries the twelve annotations for exactly 58 studies, all-or-nothing - 696 of 52,884 (study,label) cells, 1.32%. No partial annotations exist to scavenge.

So every local number in this project (0.8081 ... 0.8283) is agreement with LLM-READ REPORT LABELS, while the competition scores agreement with RADIOLOGIST ANNOTATIONS. We select epochs, members and recipes on a proxy.

NOT FIXABLE LOCALLY: the 58 are trained on at ANNOTATED_WEIGHT=3.0, so scoring them is scoring training data; held out, fold 0 gets ~12 of them with 2-7 positives per label, which is the Hanley-McNeil +/-0.17 regime knee-6xm already computed.

THE PROXY APPEARS TO COMPRESS ~2x. Two ledger rows carry both numbers: local 0.8162 -> LB 0.868, and local 0.8269 -> LB 0.888. +0.0107 local became +0.020 on the leaderboard. If that holds, the owner's 1.5% bar applied to the LB is about +0.008 locally - which would REINSTATE base (+0.0085) and put ranking (+0.0067) on the edge.

LIMITS, stated: two points, and the second row changed three things at once (augmentation fix + OneCycle + overlap TTA). Not a law. Enough to justify spending a submission to find out; not enough to re-score the ledger by.

CONSEQUENCE FOR SPENDING: 5 submissions/day, kernel pushes unlimited. The local number decides WHICH recipe to submit; only the LB decides whether it is better. Our best recipe (base + ranking, 0.8283) has never been on the LB - the 0.888 there is the old 5-fold ensemble.

title: Slice coverage: we discard a third of the band we chose to read
description:
MEASURED, 642 series across 120 studies sampled from the real corpus: slices per series median 30 (p25 25, p75 33, p95 40, max 320). The 0.20-0.80 band we read therefore holds ~18 slices on the median study, and we cache 12 of them.

So we keep 67% of the band on the median study, and 89% of series have MORE than 12 slices inside it. A third of the evidence we already decided was worth reading is being dropped before the model sees anything.

WHY THIS AND NOT ANOTHER KNOB (the 1.5% bar): a meniscal tear is visible on 2-3 slices, and five of the twelve targets are meniscus/ligament. Dropping a third of the band is a real chance of never showing the model the slices the finding lives on - that is a mechanism that can plausibly move percent, unlike a loss tweak.

COST is on the cheap axis by the cache's own docstring: bytes grow LINEARLY with slices and with the SQUARE of resolution. 20 slices = 59.7 GB against 1.2 TB free, and the filename carries the slice count so the 12-slice cache is untouched and every existing member stays reproducible.

Building now (--slices 20 --workers 12). Arm to follow: base + ranking @24 on 20 slices vs the same recipe on 12 (0.8283).

WATCH: inference averages over MORE windows with 20 slices, so the efficiency kernel's runtime goes up. That is the accuracy entry's problem, not the efficiency entry's - they are separate submissions.
close_reason: REFUTED CLEANLY, and the excuse for the first failure was wrong too. Arm Q (12 slices, max pooling) 0.8310 vs arm R (20 slices, max pooling) 0.8309 = -0.0001. Max pooling makes a group's physical thickness independent of the slice count, so this is the deconfounded test the earlier -0.0016 could not be. The thickness story - 'more slices failed because each group spans less tissue' - predicted that 20 slices would WIN once thickness was held constant. It did not. More slices inside the band buy nothing; the third of the band we discard was not carrying the findings. The 20-slice cache stays on disk (59.7 GB) and every 12-slice member remains reproducible.

title: DINOv2-large: the rung above the public frontier
description:
Every strong public notebook stops at base. The reason is the scored kernel's T4, which constrains INFERENCE only - training runs on our own 5090, and metaresearch/dinov2/PyTorch/large/1 exists (1.2 GB, 300M params, 1024-wide).

WHY THIS AND NOT ANOTHER KNOB: our own ladder says capacity and training time are the only two levers that have ever cleared the 0.0062 noise floor (small->base +0.0085, 8->24 epochs +0.0068, and they ADD: base@20 = 0.8255 vs small@8 = 0.8081). Every knob-sized idea we have tried has landed inside the floor. Large is the next rung on the one axis that pays.

RISK, stated upfront: VRAM at batch 12 (base used 13.7 of 32 GB; large is ~3.5x the parameters). If it OOMs the arm must NOT silently drop to batch 6 - we already paid for that confound once, when base ran at batch 6 against batch-12 baselines and had to be killed and requeued.

SECOND RISK: a large member may not fit the Efficiency kernel's runtime budget. That is fine and it is why two kernels exist - the accuracy entry and the efficiency entry are separate submissions, and 347 of 897 teams carry an efficiency score strictly below their public best.

Queued as /tmp/chain9.sh behind the depth bracket.

title: Ranking term: optimise the ordering the metric reads, not the calibration it discards
description:
CONFIRMED DIRECTIONALLY, NOT A RESULT. Seed 2026: 0.8272 vs 0.8205 (+0.0067). Seed 7: 0.8284 vs 0.8248 (+0.0036). On base: 0.8283 vs 0.8255 (+0.0028). Three arms, all positive.

RE-SCORED against the owner's bar (1-2% absolute, ~1.5% working, stated 2026-08-11): +0.005 is NOISE, not a finding. My earlier framing - 'the first change other than capacity to clear the noise floor' - judged it against the 0.0062 seed spread, which measures DETECTABILITY and not worth. Withdrawn.

KEPT IN THE RECIPE anyway, on cost rather than on effect: the term is free at inference, it is the exact quantity the metric scores (per-label pairwise order), and it is positive in 3/3 matched arms. It does NOT earn further seeds or a weight sweep.

Best recipe so far: base + ranking, 24 epochs = 0.8283, which is +0.0202 on the original small@8 baseline of 0.8081. The CUMULATIVE number clears the bar; no single step in it does.

Kept in the recipe on cost (free at inference, exactly the quantity the metric scores) rather than on effect - and the bead itself says it earns no further seeds and no weight sweep. Nothing actionable remains.

title: Measure EMA: is the 0.0062 seed spread a variance problem we can damp?
description:
EMA is now wired (--ema). Queued as /tmp/chain6.sh behind chain5: two arms, small@24, one-cycle, weight-floor, report_labels_v2, fold 0, seeds 2026 and 7.

Controls already on the ruler: seed 2026 = 0.8205; seed 7 = chain3 arm 3, running now.

Two seeds and not one ON PURPOSE, which is not a violation of stage-gated rigor: the claim EMA makes IS about run-to-run variance, and a single seed cannot show a variance reduction at all. The mean moving is the secondary read; the spread narrowing is the hypothesis.
close_reason:
Measured, matched, two seeds: +0.0012 (s2026) and +0.0007 (s7). Same sign twice, mean +0.0010, far inside the 0.0062 noise floor - not a lever.

No convergence gain either, and the claim that there was one is withdrawn: time to within 0.001 of each arm's own best is EMA 12 vs control 13 epochs. The apparent 2x speedup came from comparing two noisy curves at one arbitrary epoch.

No variance claim possible at n=2 (control spread 0.0043, EMA 0.0038).

KEPT for the final full-data fit regardless, on an argument the fold-0 number cannot address: --fold -1 has no holdout and keeps its LAST epoch by construction, so the shipped artefact depends on where training stopped, and the curve wanders 0.004 between epochs 13 and 24. That is variance in the deliverable, not in a fold score.

title: A missing binary reads as a passing gate: 'cmd; echo EXIT $?' reports the echo
description:
PREMISE WAS WRONG, corrected 2026-08-11. The original claim - 'nox -s gates is weaker than pre-commit' - was false. gates calls lint, which runs hygiene.mirror; the two agree.

THE REAL CAUSE: nox is not on PATH in this Git-bash (only uv/uvx, at /c/Users/User/.local/bin), and it is not a project dependency either, so 'uv run nox' fails too. The working entry is 'uvx nox -s gates'.

WHY IT LOOKED GREEN: the command was 'nox -s gates > log 2>&1; echo "GATES EXIT $?"'. A compound statement's status is the LAST command's - the echo - which always succeeds, so the harness reported exit 0. The log held one line, 'nox: command not found', and I did not read it because the wrapper said 0. Reported the gates green twice on that basis.

SAME ROOT AS knee-74x, now twice in one session (pkill, nox): a command that does not exist fails in a way that reads as success inside a compound statement.

THE RULE: never infer success from a wrapper's exit code. Grep the LOG for the tool's own success marker ('Session gates was successful'), and prefer '&&' over ';' so a missing binary short-circuits.

Nothing was verified by those runs. The commits they blessed were separately checked by the pre-commit hook set, which does run and did block once - so the tree is fine; the reporting was not.
close_reason: Rule landed in CLAUDE.md + AGENTS.md: uvx nox, verify by the tool's own success marker, '&&' not ';'. Nothing further to build; the postmortem is the deliverable.

title: Ship a single full-data fit, not a fold ensemble
description: REORDERED 2026-08-11: the full-data fit is a DELIVERABLE, not a finding. Running it before the EMA and ranking arms would spend ~40 GPU-min on a member we would re-fit if either wins. chain5 killed while still waiting; the fit runs last, with whatever recipe survives chain7.

title: Epoch budget also clears the noise floor: 8 -> 24 epochs is +0.0068 on small
description: CONFIRMED, final: 24-epoch small 0.8205 vs 8-epoch 0.8081 = +0.0124, twice the noise floor. Curve peaked around epoch 18-21 then flattened (0.8187-0.8189 at 22-23), so ~20-24 epochs is roughly the right budget for small at this data size. Larger than the encoder change (+0.0085), and a 24-epoch SMALL model beats an 8-epoch BASE one (0.8166). CONSEQUENCE: every arm in the ablation ledger was run at 8 epochs against a baseline that had not converged, so 'no measured effect' there means 'measured in the wrong regime'. The five leaderboard members are 8-epoch; retraining the same recipe at ~24 is worth about +0.012 before anything else changes.
close_reason: CONFIRMED and applied: 24 epochs is in every arm since. Ledger consequence recorded (the 8-epoch table was measured pre-convergence) and carried by knee-ghl. The question this bead asked is answered.

title: DINOv2-base clears the noise floor: +0.0085, needs seeds and more epochs
description: FINAL fold-0 ladder on report_labels_v2, all matched, floor 0.0062: small 8ep 0.8081, base 8ep 0.8166 (+0.0085), small 24ep 0.8205 (+0.0124), base 20ep 0.8255 (+0.0174). The two capacity levers ADD rather than substitute. Submission recipe: base, 20 epochs, batch 12. Five-fold retrain queued behind the label test; base submission path already dry-run verified on the host (variant resolves, mount matches, fingerprint passes). Leaderboard members are small-at-8-epochs, so this is the first change since the augmentation bug expected to move the public number.

title: Per-slice encoding with max pooling, and a CNN backbone — the only untested difference of the right size
description:
EVERY KNOB IS EXHAUSTED AND THEY ARE ALL THE SAME SIZE. Measured on this architecture: schedule +0.0061, augmentation-applied +0.0110, TTA +0.0035, intensity augmentation +0.0019, weight floor +0.0019, better labels -0.0008, 32 slices -0.018. Apart from the three defects, nothing is worth more than 0.002.

THE REMAINING GAPS ARE AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE BIGGER: our per-member holdout 0.8269 against the .903 reference's reported OOF 0.8544, and 0.888 against the leader's 0.942. Nothing measured explains either.

THE .903 RECIPE DIFFERS STRUCTURALLY, NOT BY SETTINGS:
  backbone     single-channel ImageNet EfficientNet-B3   (ours: DINOv2-small ViT, 3-channel)
  study input  3 fluid-sensitive plane-diverse series    (ours: 6 plane x weighting slots)
  pooling      MAX over slice embeddings, then MEAN over series logits
               (ours: 3 consecutive slices stacked as CHANNELS, then per-diagnosis attention over slots)

THE POOLING DIFFERENCE IS THE ONE WITH A MECHANISM WE HAVE ALREADY FELT. Our channel stacking is what made 32 inference slices FAIL (-0.018): raising the slice count over a fixed band changes each group's physical thickness, so the model sees an input distribution it never trained on. Per-slice encoding has no such coupling — which is exactly why THEY can raise slices at inference and we cannot. The same coupling plausibly limits what a fixed 12-slice budget can see: a finding is either inside a sampled 3-slice group or invisible.

WHY IT IS NOW AFFORDABLE: `StudyModel` already takes its backbone as an injected `nn.Module` (structural, not a named protocol — written that way for exactly this), and timm 1.0.26 is in Kaggle's image, so an EfficientNet needs no wheel. What has to change is the bag layout and `_pool`.

SCOPE, and it is genuinely two experiments that should not be confused:
  1. AGGREGATION: keep DINOv2, encode each slice independently, max over slices. Isolates pooling.
  2. BACKBONE: keep the aggregation, swap the encoder. Isolates the encoder family.
Run 1 first — it is the one with a mechanism we have already observed, and it does not need a new model mount.

CAVEAT THAT MUST NOT BE FORGOTTEN: at ~0.002 per knob and an unmeasured noise floor, a single fold cannot resolve a small win here either. This is worth doing only because the hypothesised effect is 0.02-0.03, not 0.002 — if it lands in the noise, it is a refutation, not a tuning opportunity.
close_reason: REFUTED at the predicted size: per-slice max +0.0018 vs 0.0012 noise floor, for 3x encoder cost, on a matched pair (0.8099 vs 0.8081). The mechanism was also wrong - 32-slice inference costs the same -0.01 under BOTH poolings, so channel-stacking's thickness coupling was not why the wide read hurt. Backbone swap (experiment 2) not run: experiment 1 was the one with an observed mechanism and it did not survive.

title: We train on the second-worst public label table; a better one is free
description:
MEASURED ON THE 58 GOLD STUDIES (2026-08-11), mean per-finding AUC of each public reader against the expert annotations:

  pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels      0.8705   <- WHAT WE TRAIN ON
  stevenleehans llm_labels_v2        0.8905
  stevenleehans llm_labels_v4_blend  0.8982   <- +0.028, free, already public
  lixin73 report_labels_gpt56sol     0.8431

Per finding the gaps are much larger than the mean suggests: Synovitis 0.695 (pilkwang) against 0.805, Contusion 0.756 against 0.862, Lateral Meniscus 0.844 against 0.886. Those are three of our four weakest labels on the holdout, and each costs a full 1/12 of the competition metric.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE NUMBER: the .903 notebook states plainly that 'the image model is downstream of label quality'. We have been tuning the model (schedule, augmentation, TTA) against labels that are 0.028 worse than the best freely available ones, so every one of those measurements was made against a handicapped target.

FUSION IS REFUTED FOR OUR READERS, which is worth recording because the .903 system's headline mechanism is fusion:
  mean of all four        0.8938
  rank-mean of all four   0.8966
  rank-mean of top three  0.8952
  best single (steven_v4) 0.8982   <- still the winner
Averaging drags the best table toward the weaker ones, and v4_blend is ALREADY a blend, so there is little independent signal left to add. Their fusion presumably worked because their private Qwen reader was independent of pilkwang's; ours are not.

DO NOT hand-pick a per-finding winner. The oracle that does scores 0.9016, but it is chosen on the same 57 studies it is scored on, and at these counts a per-finding AUC carries roughly +/-0.09. That is the same trap the annotation check sets (identical members scoring 0.7356 to 0.9164 on it).

ACTION: retrain on steven_v4_blend and re-measure. Every recipe result so far (schedule +0.0061, augmentation +0.011) should be re-confirmed against the better labels, because a gain measured against noisier targets can shrink or grow when the targets improve.
notes:
SWAP NEEDS NO CODE (2026-08-11). `Targets.load` already handles the better table unchanged:

  report_labels_v2 (ours)   7 distinct target values, 12 __conf columns, mean weight 0.692
  llm_labels_v4_blend       186 distinct target values, NO __conf columns, mean weight 1.026

The absence of __conf is not a gap to fill. pilkwang's table carries a coarse score (five levels) plus a separate confidence; v4_blend carries a genuinely continuous score, so the uncertainty lives IN the target rather than beside it. BCE against 0.5 already pulls weakly in both directions, so adding a derived confidence would double-count the same doubt. It is also exactly what the .903 recipe does: 'BCE-with-logits on fused soft labels'.

CONSEQUENCE FOR AN OPEN ISSUE: with uniform weights, knee-9sy (the 0.25 weight floor) becomes moot under these labels — a floor only matters when some weights are zero, and none are. It stays open only for the old table.

QUEUED, so the GPU never idles between the five-fold run finishing and the ablations starting:
  A  fold 0, v4_blend labels, otherwise the recipe that scored 0.8202  -> isolates LABELS
  B  fold 0, v4_blend + intensity augmentation                        -> both changes together
  C  fold 0, old labels + intensity augmentation                      -> isolates AUGMENTATION

A, B and C against the 0.8202 baseline give both main effects and the interaction from three runs rather than four, because the baseline already exists.
METHODOLOGY BUG IN MY OWN ABLATION, caught mid-flight (2026-08-11).

`train.py` used ONE label table for both training and scoring, so the queued arms would have been measured with different rulers: the 0.8202 baseline was scored against pilkwang targets, while arm A (trained on v4_blend) would have been scored against v4_blend targets. A holdout AUC can rise simply because the labels agree with THEMSELVES more, and I would have read that as a better model.

FIX: `--eval-labels` separates the ruler from the training signal, defaulting to `--labels` so existing behaviour is unchanged.

RULER CHOSEN DELIBERATELY: pilkwang for every arm — the table the baseline used, and NOT the table the interesting arm trains on. A v4-trained model therefore earns no self-agreement credit; it is judged by the other reader. That makes the test conservative: it can understate v4's benefit but cannot manufacture one. If training on v4 improves a pilkwang-scored holdout, the labels are genuinely better rather than merely more self-consistent.

ARMS (fold 0, all scored on pilkwang):
  baseline  train pilkwang               0.8202  (already measured)
  A         train v4_blend               -> LABELS, conservative
  C         train pilkwang + intensity   -> AUGMENTATION, clean
  B         train v4_blend + intensity   -> both

45 minutes of GPU were killed to fix this rather than spending them on numbers that could not be compared.
ARM A RESULT — BETTER LABELS ARE NEUTRAL HERE (2026-08-11), which does not support the thesis I filed this issue on.

  baseline  train pilkwang, eval pilkwang   0.8202
  A         train v4_blend, eval pilkwang   0.8194   (-0.0008, i.e. flat)

The label tables differ by +0.028 in agreement with the 58 gold studies, and that difference did NOT translate into a better model on this measurement.

WHAT THE RESULT DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH, since the ruler is not neutral:
- The ruler is pilkwang, so the BASELINE enjoys a self-agreement advantage that arm A does not. 'Flat on a ruler tilted toward the baseline' is therefore weak evidence that v4 is at least as good, and is NOT evidence that it is worse.
- Equally, it is not the win the label-quality measurement suggested. BCE against soft targets is fairly robust to label noise, and both tables are derived from the SAME reports by different readers — so the readers' disagreement may be concentrated on studies whose reports are genuinely ambiguous, where neither label is reliable and the image cannot settle it either.

THE TEST THAT WOULD SETTLE IT is a cross-fitted evaluation on the 58 gold studies: each gold study scored only by the fold-model that held it out, for both label choices. Fold 0's holdout contains roughly a dozen gold studies, far too few alone, so this needs all five folds per arm — about 2.5 hours of GPU. That is the honest price of an unbiased ruler, and it is worth paying only if the augmentation arm does not turn out to be the larger lever.

DO NOT quietly switch the training labels on the strength of a label-quality number. The measurement that matters is the model's, and it says nothing so far.
CORRECTION (2026-08-11): closed as 'null' on a single-fold matched pair, but seed variance on the same fold is +/-0.012 while these effects are +/-0.002. The correct verdict is NOT DETECTABLE at n=1, not null. Neither is worth re-running bigger — resolving 0.002 against 0.012 needs ~36 paired runs — but the record should not claim more than it measured. See knee-uxg.
close_reason: Null on the model's own measurement (-0.0013 mean) despite +0.028 label quality against gold. Do not switch training labels on a label-quality number alone.

title: Augmentation was written, tested, and never called by the training loop
description:
FOUND 2026-08-11. `Trainer.augment` exists, is unit-tested, and `fit_epoch` NEVER CALLED IT. Every run to this point — all five folds and BOTH leaderboard submissions — trained with zero augmentation.

EVIDENCE IT MATTERED: the 40-epoch OneCycle curve peaks near epoch 16 and then declines monotonically (0.8143 -> 0.8043 by ep36). That is textbook overfitting, and it explains how they train 60 epochs where we degrade after 16.

WHY BOTH GATES MISSED IT, which is the part worth keeping:
- vulture (dead code) saw the method as USED, because its unit test references it.
- the mirror gate saw it as TESTED, because it has a `test_augment`.
A method can therefore be fully covered and completely disconnected. The gates check that a method exists, is referenced and is tested; none of them checks that the CALLER calls it.

FIX: `fit_epoch` now routes every batch through `augment_bag`, which converts uint8 -> float, warps, and converts back so `StudyModel.forward` (and therefore the fingerprint) is untouched. Slots are warped independently: they are separate acquisitions of one knee, not one volume, so a shared jitter would imply a registration that does not exist.

NEW TEST that would have caught it: `test_fit_epoch_augments` wraps `augment_bag` and asserts the training loop actually calls it. The general lesson: test the CALLER, not only the callee.
notes:
FIXED AND MEASURED (2026-08-11). Fold 0, every run matched on seed and data, only the recipe differing:

  constant LR, no aug, 16 ep   0.8092   <- the recipe BOTH leaderboard submissions used
  OneCycle,    no aug, 16 ep   0.8153   (+0.0061 from the schedule)
  OneCycle,    no aug, 40 ep   0.8181   best, but the tail DECLINES to 0.8043 by ep36
  OneCycle,    aug,    30 ep   0.8201   best, and the tail is FLAT (0.8172-0.8181 through ep29)

+0.0109 over the submitted recipe, and the overfitting is GONE rather than merely checkpointed around: the unaugmented 40-epoch run fell 0.014 from its peak, the augmented 30-epoch run falls 0.003.

That closes about half the 0.0236 per-member gap to their 0.8398, from two changes that were already written in our own code and simply not connected.

SIDE EFFECT WORTH KEEPING: epoch time fell 40s -> 30s from the memmap indexing fix (images[b, :, s:s+G] in one op rather than images[b][:, :, s:s+G], which materialised all twelve slices to use three). So the corrected recipe at 30 epochs costs about the same wall-clock as the old one at 16.
close_reason: fit_epoch now routes pixels through augment_bag; measured +0.0110 on fold 0, and a test asserts the CALLER not just the callee

title: Medial beats lateral on both pairs — is our laterality recovery wrong, or is it the labels?
description:
Per-label holdout AUC, our fold 0:

    Lateral Meniscus 0.742  vs  Medial Meniscus 0.785   (-0.043)
    Lateral OA       0.774  vs  Medial OA       0.840   (-0.066)
    MCL              0.747  vs  ACL             0.821

BOTH medial/lateral pairs favour medial, and the side-defined targets are exactly the ones a broken laterality normalisation would damage. That is a hypothesis, not a finding — medial pathology is also commoner and more often named in reports, which would produce the same asymmetry through label quality alone.

IT IS CHEAP TO SETTLE, and the audit found why: the diagnostic needs only HEADERS, not pixels. `Acquisition` already carries `laterality_tag` and `centre_x`, so resolving how each study's side was decided is ~24k header reads (~15 s with 20 workers). No cache rebuild.

MEASUREMENT: split the holdout three ways — side from the TAG, side from GEOMETRY, side UNRESOLVED — and compare the medial-minus-lateral AUC gap in each.
  - gap flat across all three  -> it is the labels; laterality is fine; this lead is dead.
  - gap worse on the geometry-resolved half -> our recovery is wrong, and it is worth more than any ensemble.
  - gap worse on the unresolved half -> those studies are being fed unmirrored and should be handled, not ignored.

The cache does NOT currently persist which rule decided each study, which is itself worth fixing once this is answered.
notes:
REFUTED (2026-08-11) — and cleanly, which is why it was worth running first.

PROVENANCE over 4407 studies (headers only, ~90s): tag 2203 (50.0%), geometry 2132 (48.4%), unresolved 72 (1.6%). On the 2135 studies where BOTH are available they agree on 98.6% (their notebook claimed ~97% for the same rule, so this validates the recovery on our corpus).

MEDIAL-MINUS-LATERAL AUC GAP, holdout of fold 0, split by how the side was decided:
  all (909)              meniscus +0.042   OA +0.060
  side from TAG (454)             +0.046      +0.036
  side from GEOMETRY (436)        +0.041      +0.085
  left knees, untouched (431)     +0.071      +0.074
  right knees, MIRRORED (459)     +0.015      +0.035

TWO REASONS THE HYPOTHESIS DIES:
1. Geometry-resolved studies show the SAME asymmetry as tag-resolved ones, so the recovery rule is not introducing it.
2. Decisively, the asymmetry is SMALLER on the knees we actually mirror (+0.015/+0.035) than on the ones we leave alone (+0.071/+0.074). A broken mirror would do the opposite.

So laterality is exonerated and the medial>lateral asymmetry is most likely prevalence/label driven: medial pathology is commoner and more often named in a report, so its derived labels are both denser and cleaner.

HONEST LIMIT: at ~450 studies per group these gaps carry roughly +/-0.02-0.03, so the tag-vs-geometry comparison is solid (it is the same number twice) while the left-vs-right split is suggestive rather than proven.

A METHOD BUG THIS FOUND, in the diagnostic itself: the first run computed the geometric side from only the UNTAGGED series of each study, which made 'both available' mean 'studies whose series disagree about having a tag' - a biased subsample of 74 that read as 86.5% agreement. Recomputing geometry from every series gave 2135 studies at 98.6%. The lesson generalises: when comparing two estimators, both must see the same input.
close_reason: Refuted: the asymmetry is identical across tag- and geometry-resolved studies and SMALLER on the mirrored knees. Laterality is exonerated; the cause is most likely label prevalence.

title: Overlap TTA at inference — implemented, free, and we submitted without it
description:
`Ensemble.predict_member` already takes `overlap: bool = False`, and both kernels call it without the argument. So both submissions averaged over 4 DISJOINT windows while their own inference path used 10 OVERLAPPING ones.

Costs one keyword argument and 2.5x a 0.3 s per-study step — against a 542 s fixed kernel cost, that is nothing. No retraining, no new decode: the cache already holds the slices.

Caveat worth measuring rather than assuming: the out-of-fold ablation found DISJOINT windows matched their stored predictions better (0.025) than overlapping (0.042). That was a statement about reproducing their OOF, not about which scores better. Run both against the same holdout locally before spending a submission.
notes:
MEASURED ON OUR OWN HOLDOUT (2026-08-11, fold 0, member_fold0):
  middle window only (1)   0.8092
  disjoint windows (4)     0.8180
  overlapping windows (10) 0.8205

So overlap is worth +0.0025 over disjoint and +0.0113 over a single window - free, no retraining, and the cache already holds the slices. Both submitted kernels used the DEFAULT overlap=False, so both left this on the table.

This also resolves the caveat: the out-of-fold ablation preferred DISJOINT because that reproduced THEIR stored predictions, which is a statement about matching their pipeline, not about which scores better. On our own holdout, overlapping wins. The two results do not conflict - they answer different questions.
close_reason: Measured (+0.0025) and enabled in both kernels: overlap=OVERLAP_TTA.

title: OneCycleLR: the plateau at epoch 12 is a missing schedule, not a missing epoch
description:
MEASURED: our five folds peak at epochs 13/13/10/12/11 and gain +0.0002/+0.0106/-0.0003/+0.0035/+0.0024 over their final five epochs. Training is saturated at ~12 epochs, so "they ran 60 epochs and we ran 16" does NOT explain the per-member gap (ours 0.8162, theirs 0.8398). Running longer at a constant learning rate would buy nothing.

AUDIT FOUND WHY: they wrap AdamW in

    torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr=[LR_BACKBONE, LR_HEAD], total_steps=EPOCHS * (len(tr) // BATCH), pct_start=0.15)

We have no schedule at all — constant 1e-3 head / 8e-6 backbone. A constant LR that plateaus at epoch 12 while a one-cycle run keeps improving to 60 is exactly the shape you would expect, and it is the single most likely cause of the per-member gap.

PROVES IT: retrain fold 0 with OneCycle, same seed, same everything else. If the holdout peak moves past 0.8092 AND the peak epoch moves late, the schedule was the cause. If it plateaus at 12 again, the cause is elsewhere and this is closed.
notes:
CONFIRMED, then partly superseded (2026-08-11). Fold 0, matched — same seed, same data, only the schedule differing:

  constant LR,  16 epochs   0.8092  (peak ep13)
  OneCycleLR,   16 epochs   0.8153  (peak ep12)   +0.0061
  OneCycleLR,   40 epochs   0.8181  best, but the curve PEAKS near ep16 (0.8143) and then declines
                                     monotonically: 0.8118 / 0.8101 / 0.8071 / 0.8061 / 0.8043

So the schedule is a real +0.0061, and MORE EPOCHS IS NOT THE LEVER: past ~16-20 the model overfits. Their 60 epochs is not something to copy directly.

WHY THEY CAN TRAIN 60 EPOCHS AND WE CANNOT — see knee-<AUG>: our `augment` was never called. Every run to this point, including both submissions, trained with ZERO augmentation. The declining tail of the 40-epoch curve is what unregularised training looks like.

OFF-BY-ONE PAID FOR: total_steps used `len(training) // batch`, but our batcher KEEPS the final partial batch while theirs drops it. OneCycleLR raised on the last step of the whole run — after every epoch had been logged, before the checkpoint was written. Fixed with a ceiling rather than by discarding data.
close_reason: Confirmed +0.0061 and shipped; more epochs refuted as a lever (the 40-epoch tail declines without augmentation).

title: Leak-safe validation: split by report-text hash
description:
Some reports are byte-identical across studies (a template read for an unremarkable knee), so every study in such a group gets the SAME derived target vector. Splitting a group across the divide scores the model on a target whose source it trained on.

Assign studies by a hash of the report text so duplicate groups stay whole. Hold out one fifth, fixed rather than rotated.

TWO REFERENCES, TWO MEANINGS: the holdout measures agreement with derived targets and has the numbers to select epoch and recipe. The annotation check measures agreement with a radiologist - what the competition scores - but only annotated studies inside the holdout may be used, and there are too few, so it is REPORTED and never allowed to arbitrate. Annotated studies stay in training at elevated weight, which is exactly why the check must exclude them.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, train.csv, 4407 studies): 4276 distinct reports, so 177 studies sit in a duplicate group. Group sizes: 27 pairs, 10 triples, one of 4, four of 5, one of 6, one of 12, one of 14, one of 37.

The largest group (37 studies) is a Turkish all-normal template: 'Diz eklemi ici sivi miktari normal. Capraz ve yan baglar normal...'. Next are Spanish templates at 14 and 12.

So the leak is real but bounded - 4% of studies. Splitting by report hash costs nothing and removes it; the 37-group alone would otherwise straddle the divide.
EMPIRICAL SUPPORT FOR 'THE ANNOTATION CHECK MUST NOT ARBITRATE' (2026-08-10, from the 20 published members):

Members differing ONLY by fold and seed - same architecture, same data, same recipe - report annotation-check scores from 0.7356 to 0.9164. That is a 0.18 spread on a metric that is supposed to measure the same thing, and it matches the Hanley-McNeil prediction (SE ~0.09 at A~0.8 with single-digit positives) almost exactly.

Their holdout scores over the same 20 members span only 0.8279 to 0.8600 - a 0.03 spread, six times tighter.

There is also structure, not just noise: every fold-2 member has a HIGH holdout (0.857-0.860) and a LOW annot (0.736-0.795). The annotated studies are distributed unevenly across folds, so which fold a member held out changes what its annotation check even measures.

So: select on the holdout, report the annotation check, and never let a 0.18-wide instrument arbitrate a 0.01 decision.
close_reason: ReportFolds.assign hashes the REPORT TEXT so duplicate template reports never straddle the split; measured leak was 4 percent of studies. Split seed is separate from the model seed (--split-seed) after the bug where seed 7's fold-0 holdout shared only 192 of 909 studies with seed 2026's.

title: Slice ordering from geometry, never from file name
description:
Order each series by k = p.n where n = r_x cross r_y from ImageOrientationPatient and p = ImagePositionPatient. InstanceNumber is the fallback where geometry tags are missing (it tracks k up to sign, but interleaved/multi-echo acquisitions number out of spatial order and it is not signed in patient coordinates).

WHY: file names are SOP Instance UIDs - unique, not ordered. Sorting by them is reported at rho ~ 0.01 against physical position, and it fails SILENTLY: three-channel adjacent slices become three unrelated cross-sections, the middle of the stack becomes a random subset, and laterality reversal becomes a no-op.

PROVES: compute Spearman rho between filename order and geometric k on a sample of our series. Expect ~0.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, one 186-slice Philips series): Spearman rho(filename order, geometric k) = -0.0106. Filename order carries no anatomical information whatsoever.

Geometry tags are present on every slice of the sample: ImagePositionPatient 186/186, ImageOrientationPatient 186/186. So the exact ordering is available and the InstanceNumber fallback may be rarely needed - measure the tag-presence rate corpus-wide before relying on that.

k spans -68.6 .. 97.9 mm over the stack.
close_reason: acquisition.py orders slices by geometry via the through-plane projection k = p.(rx x ry), never by file name.

title: Series -> slot routing, with Fluid_Sensitive/Fat_Suppression recovered from the header
description:
Six slots: SAG_FLUID_FS, COR_FLUID_FS, AX_FLUID_FS, SAG_FLUID_NOFS, COR_T1, SAG_T1, plus a per-slot presence mask (a study rarely has all six).

MECHANISM: the shipped Fluid_Sensitive/Fat_Suppression columns are reported to agree on every training row, i.e. they carry ONE axis where the names claim two. Recover both from the header: weighting from TR/TE (T1: TR<~800; T2: TR>~800 and TE>~60; PD: TR>~800 and TE<~60), settled by ScanningSequence first because gradient echo breaks the TR rule; fat suppression from SeriesDescription/SequenceName/ScanOptions, falling back to TR/TE.

PROVES: on OUR copy of train_series.csv, measure the agreement rate between the two shipped columns. If it is 100%, the degeneracy is confirmed and recovery is mandatory, not optional.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, train_series.csv, 24371 rows): Fluid_Sensitive == Fat_Suppression on 1.000000 of rows. The crosstab is a clean diagonal - 10361 at (0,0), 14010 at (1,1), zero off-diagonal.

The two columns carry ONE axis, not two. Recovering both from the header (TR/TE/ScanningSequence for weighting, SeriesDescription/ScanOptions for fat-sat) is therefore mandatory, not an optimisation.

Corroborated by the sample series: SeriesDescription 'AX PD FS MPR L' with TR 1100 / TE 23 - TR>800 and TE<60 reads PD by the rule, and ScanOptions 'FS' gives the suppression independently. The rule reproduces the description.

Planes: Sagittal 9864, Coronal 8609, Axial 5898. Series per study mean 5.53, max 14 - so the six-slot scheme has real material to route.
IMPLEMENTED + MEASURED FROM THE PIXELS (2026-08-10). On 150 random series our recovered fat-suppression agrees with the shipped Fat_Suppression column on 99.3%, but our recovered fluid-sensitivity agrees with the shipped Fluid_Sensitive column on only 78.7%.

So the shipped pair is the FAT-SAT axis alone, wearing two names - the earlier finding that the two columns are identical on 1.000000 of rows said they carry one axis; this says WHICH one. The non-fat-suppressed pool is 40 T1 against 32 PD/T2, so routing on the shipped flags would put fluid-weighted series into the T1 slots for about a fifth of the corpus, and the presence mask would assert a sequence that was never acquired.
close_reason: slots.py routes on fluid-sensitivity and fat-suppression recovered from TR/TE/ScanningSequence and SeriesDescription/SequenceName/ScanOptions. Confirmed necessary: the shipped Fluid_Sensitive and Fat_Suppression columns agree on 1.000 of all 24371 series - they are the same column, so routing on them would be routing on one bit.

title: Graft: inference-only kernel from pilkwang's mounted weights -> LB floor
description:
Mount pilkwang/rsna-knee-weights + pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels + metaresearch/dinov2/PyTorch/small/1, run inference over the mounted test set, submit.

WHY: needs no local data and no training, and turns the field's public plateau (~0.899) into a measured number on OUR submission path. Same move as the biohub pilkwang graft.

HONESTY: the score is his result, not ours. Record it in comp/SUBMISSIONS.md as a graft; it must never appear in a README as our number, and it is a floor to build past, never an end state.
notes:
GRAFT, PHASE A IN PROGRESS (2026-08-10).

The weights manifest is fully self-describing: 20 members = 5 folds x 4 seeds, ALL one config (336px, 12 slices, group 3, crop 130mm, dinov2-small, cls_mean pool, prior false, unfreeze_last 6). One pixel_group, so a single decode serves all twenty. Their own numbers: holdout mean 0.8398 (min 0.8279, max 0.8600), annot mean 0.8375 (min 0.7356, max 0.9164).

Split into two phases because they have different prerequisites:
- PHASE A (no pixels needed): port the architecture and prove it faithful against the manifest's stored fingerprints. Done in kneemri/{model,slot_head,members}.py; comp/kernels/kneemri-graft-verify is the oracle.
- PHASE B (needs pixels): the data layer - slot routing, geometric ordering, laterality, crop/resample, decode-once cache. That is the bulk of the public notebook and wants local data, because debugging it one kernel push at a time is the slow way to do it.

LICENCE: both pilkwang datasets are CC0-1.0. The competition's own external-data clause is still unread (knee-0s6) - so NO SUBMISSION until that is settled.
PHASE A COMPLETE (2026-08-10): the architecture port is PROVEN faithful.

comp/kernels/kneemri-graft-verify v6: 20/20 members loaded and reproduced their stored fingerprints. Worst max|diff| = 4.65e-06 against a 2e-3 tolerance - a 430x margin, and squarely in the ~1e-5 GPU-numeric-noise band the tolerance was set between. Our StudyModel computes the same function these weights were fitted to; any error in pooling, ImageNet normalisation, resize or head would have moved it by order one.

Four kernel pushes were spent on mount/packaging shape, all cheap (pushes unlimited, no submission spent):
  v1-v3: mounts nest by kind (/kaggle/input/{competitions,datasets,models}/...) and a --dir-mode zip upload is expanded WITHOUT its wrapping directory, so kneemri_src/ never exists.
  v4: jaxtyping absent from Kaggle's image (see knee-61q note).
  v5: published checkpoints wrap weights under 'model' beside epoch/holdout/annot/config/oof/fingerprint.

REMAINS FOR THE GRAFT: Phase B, the data layer (knee-64b, knee-7ve, knee-e5e, knee-b0c, knee-37l). No submission until knee-0s6's external-data clause is read.
SUBMITTED (2026-08-10, submission 55415728): 20 published CC0 members through OUR data layer, rank-averaged per label. Kernel loaded and fingerprint-checked all 20 in 575s; 3 public test studies decoded in 3s and predicted in 5s, so ~1s decode + ~1.7s predict per study extrapolates to well under an hour for a hidden set of ~1000. Status PENDING - a code competition re-runs the kernel against the hidden test set, so scoring takes as long as the run.

PHASE B COMPLETE: the data layer is built and proven against the members' own out-of-fold predictions (max|diff| 0.025, per-study correlation 0.99, under DISJOINT windows - located by ablation: overlapping 0.042, single central window 0.163, fp16-vs-fp32 0.0004 i.e. irrelevant).
GRAFT SCORED: 0.888 public LB (submission 55415728, 2026-08-10).

What the number buys, beyond being a floor:
- The submission path is PROVEN end to end against the hidden test set, not just against the 3 public studies.
- It prices OUR DATA LAYER in leaderboard units. The weights are pilkwang published members, identical to what the public forks run; the only difference is our pipeline reading the pixels. The best public fork sits near 0.899, so our reading of the same weights costs about 0.011.
- That agrees in direction and rough magnitude with the 0.025 out-of-fold residual measured locally. Two independent measurements of the same imperfection, which promotes the slot tie-break hypothesis from a shrug to a lead worth chasing: when two candidate series have equal slice counts, his pandas sort_values picks the first in frame order and our max() picks the first in list order, and a different series in a slot changes the image the head reads.

NEXT MEASUREMENT that would settle it: re-run the OOF oracle while logging which series each slot got, and count how often a study has a tie at all. If ties are rare and the residual persists, the cause is elsewhere.
close_reason: DONE and SCORED: 0.888 public LB (submission 55415728, 2026-08-10). Phase A proven faithful (20/20 fingerprints, worst max|diff| 4.65e-06 against a 2e-3 tolerance), Phase B data layer built and proven against the members' own OOF predictions. Submission path proven end to end against the hidden test set. Remaining thread - the ~0.011 data-layer residual and the slot tie-break hypothesis - carved out as knee-evn. FORCE-CLOSED over its blocker knee-0s6: the submission was spent BEFORE that gate cleared, which is recorded on knee-0s6 rather than hidden here.

title: torch.compile and bf16: the last throughput levers, and why they must land at a boundary
description:
AUDIT 2026-08-11 of what we do and do not use, prompted by the owner asking directly.

IN USE:
  - Gradient checkpointing (--recompute-activations, added today). MEASURED: 32 GB -> 19 GB with the loss untouched, and it is what let the whole-stack arm fit at all.
  - SDPA fused attention - already on by default under transformers 5.15 (_attn_implementation reports 'sdpa'), so attention matrices are never materialised. Checked before assuming.

NOT IN USE:
  - bf16. We run fp16 autocast plus a GradScaler, which is autocast's CUDA default rather than a decision anyone made.
  - torch.compile. Nowhere in the tree.
  - TF32. Never set.

WHAT EACH IS WORTH, on this hardware and this loop:
  - bf16: SAME matmul throughput as fp16 on Blackwell. The win is robustness - no GradScaler, no scale-collapse - not speed. We have seen no NaN trouble, so this is insurance rather than a fix.
  - TF32: affects fp32 matmuls only, and under autocast the encoder already runs fp16. Near zero here.
  - torch.compile: the ONLY remaining double-digit lever. 10-30% is typical for a ViT. Compatible with our checkpointing because use_reentrant=False was chosen deliberately.

RISKS FOR COMPILE, to check rather than assume: the final batch of an epoch is partial, so the shape change triggers a recompilation every epoch unless batches drop_last or pad; and the supervised() two-readout path returns a tuple from one encoder pass, which is exactly the sort of graph that can force a break.

WHY NONE OF THIS LANDS MID-QUEUE: every control in the ledger - the 0.8272 baseline, arm Q at 0.8310, the whole-stack arm now running against them - was measured under fp16 with eager kernels. Changing precision or kernel fusion changes numerics, so an arm run afterwards is no longer strictly matched to the control it is quoted against. This project has already paid for one unmatched comparison when a 'new best' turned out to be a seed change.

THE PROTOCOL: land them together at a natural boundary, then run ONE matched arm (same fold, same seed, same recipe) under the new settings and confirm the score is unchanged within the 0.0062 noise floor. If it moves, the speed is not worth an unexplained score change. Record the seconds-per-epoch delta in experiments/README.md so the cost of the guarantee is visible.

Pairs with knee-5f0 (the batch/VRAM sweep): both are throughput work that must be measured on an idle card, and both should be done in one sitting rather than trickled in.

title: Runs are compared by grepping logs: no metrics file, no experiment tracker
description:
RAISED BY THE OWNER 2026-08-11, asking about mlflow/tqdm/periodic logging.

WHAT LANDED IMMEDIATELY: kneemri/heartbeat.py. One line per epoch could not distinguish a slow run from a wedged one, and that cost a quarter of an hour today - a whole-stack arm sat thrashing on a VRAM overflow and the only evidence was the card's power draw. The heartbeat reports step, loss and images/s every 30 seconds, paced by SECONDS because step cost varies ~20x across arms.

TQDM WAS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, on a specific ground rather than taste: every arm's output is redirected to a file. A progress bar in a file is a trail of carriage returns - the HuggingFace weight-loading bar already litters every log we own, and it is the reason grepping arm logs needs a 'grep -v Loading weights'. A log line is the right instrument when the reader is a file, not a terminal.

WHAT IS STILL MISSING, and what it costs: there is no machine-readable record of a run. Comparing arms today means grepping 'best holdout' out of a dozen log files scattered across /tmp and processed/experiments, by hand, and the ledger in experiments/README.md is maintained by ME rather than by the runs. That is how a result gets misattributed - it already happened once, when a 'new best' turned out to be a seed change.

THE CHEAP FIX, and the one I would do first: a metrics.jsonl beside each checkpoint - one line per epoch with {epoch, loss, auc, seconds, lr, vram_peak}. No server, no daemon, nothing to run; it is greppable, diffable, and plots from pandas in three lines. Data stays out of the repo like every other artefact.

ON MLFLOW SPECIFICALLY: it would give run comparison and a UI, and it costs a local server plus a tracking directory plus a dependency, and it wants to own the run lifecycle. For a single-machine project whose arms are already committed shell scripts, that is a lot of machinery for what a JSONL and pandas provide. I would only reach for it if we start running many arms per day and need to slice them by hyperparameter interactively. Worth revisiting then, not now.

NOT URGENT while the queue is one arm deep - it is a workflow cost, not a score cost.

title: Three arms lost in one afternoon: one unexplained, one unproven, one I killed by editing it mid-run
description:

1. ARM U (composed shipping candidate) died at epoch 7 of 24 and PRINTED 'ARM U DONE'. Cause unknown and will stay unknown: it ran from the old /tmp script, which piped into grep with no tee, so the traceback was discarded. The tee fix had been committed hours earlier and was never applied to the arm already in flight - a fix that does not reach running work is not yet a fix.
